title: I tested an LLM as a trade-idea generator for a month. Here's where it actually helped
author: zohaahmed1
selftext:
Not a hype post and not an anti-AI rant, just what happened when I tested it properly, because I keep seeing people ask chatbots what to buy tomorrow.



As a trade-idea generator it was bad, in predictable ways. It doesn't see live prices unless you feed them in, so plenty of its levels were stale. It states things with the same confidence whether it's right or making them up, including indicator values it never calculated. And it leans on whatever narrative dominated its training data, which is usually the opposite of what you want at turning points. I logged 40 of its ideas on paper and the result was roughly a coin flip before costs.



Where it was genuinely useful was everything around the trading. Code, for one. It wrote most of the scaffolding for an MT5 EA in MQL5 and a Python script that pulls my trade history into a dataframe. Both needed fixing, but it saved hours.



It was also good at journal analysis. I pasted three months of trades with my notes and asked it to group losses by setup, time of day and what I'd written before entering. It spotted that most of my worst trades came straight after two losses in a row, which I knew vaguely but had never quantified.



For testing the EA I use an AvaTrade demo since that's where my live account is, but the same code runs on any MT5 broker, IC Markets or anyone else. Whatever you use, run anything an LLM wrote on a demo for a few weeks first. It will happily write code that compiles fine and does something slightly different from what you asked.



So my rule now is LLM for code, research summaries and journal analysis, never for the decision itself. Curious whether anyone here has found a setup where it adds real edge on the signal side.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: The “worst trades after two losses” finding needs a denominator before it becomes actionable. In the three-month journal, compare loss rate and average expectancy after zero, one, and two consecutive losses, while controlling for setup and time of day. Otherwise the LLM may simply have rediscovered that a bad session contains clustered losses. I’d also preserve the exact 40 paper ideas, contemporaneous prices, and prompts, then score whether stale levels or invented indicators explain the coin-flip result. That failure taxonomy would be more informative than the aggregate hit rate.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
stale levels were the worst of it for me too. a model asked for a price nobody handed it will just make one up, and that gets you most of the way to a coin flip.

40 ideas is thin though. replaying a written rule over past bars, blind to what came after, is what I built Quantradin to do, on paper and free. quantradin.com

did you log the levels it gave or only the direction?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Useful split, and logging all 40 ideas on paper before judging is the right way to test it. For the signal side, the one place I've seen it help is reading text, like news or filings, and tagging it so a fixed rule can use the tag, with the rule and the sizing kept in code. The check is whether the tag changes results compared with the same rules without it. Cymetica's Event Cards turn a news event into a sourced, tradable basket, which is one example of using text as an input.

comments.author: lulubike
comments.body:
I'm experimenting with decision side and It looks promising to me. I experiment with various combinations of  candlestick data, some indicators, and also charts as images in multiple time frames along with trading strategy description. LLMs need to be "grounded" with data to be  reliable.   
I also use it for strategy development and validation. Its also most useful when you define a strict validation workflow and with good, reliable tooling around.

replies.author: Antfrombeliefstate
replies.body: Have you compared it with simple rules using the exact same inputs? Also curious if you're using it to read news and research, or mainly charts.

comments.author: itlogicpartnersllc
comments.body: the journal analysis angle seems far more practical than asking an llm what to buy. quantifying behavioral patterns you already suspect can reveal weaknesses that are easy to overlook.

comments.author: TrifactorMacro
comments.body:
Key rules that I followed were to 1) make the system 100% mechanical and rule based.
2) give signals on the higher time frames. In my case weekly
3) easy to backtest - in a sense that I get data that is unambiguous so the analysis can be replicable
4) trade limited amount of assets and with limited moving parts
5) fit my lifestyle - I am nearly 40 with 2 kids and a 9-to-5. I need to be able to sleep I nigth and I want to as little maintenance as possible

The system is taking the results on Friday (for the market close)  and  on Sunday close ( for BTC) and makes a descison for Monday morning. Repeat next week. 
Simplistic is the key when using ai. And a lot of different backtests, analysis, stress testing.

comments.author: ApartmentOk3498
comments.body: journal analysis is prob where llms help most, way more useful than asking what to buy

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
The EA scaffolding is a useful example of AI assisting development without owning the trading decision. I’d turn each intended behavior into a small replay case—especially signal timing, stop updates, rejected orders and reconnects—then compare that trace with what the generated code actually does. Compilation alone cannot establish that match.



We’re QATS. If you want to try a visual version of that workflow for a separate prop-perpetuals setup, our AI-assisted Bot Builder exposes entry/exit blocks and backtesting: [https://prop.qats.us/bot-builder](https://prop.qats.us/bot-builder) . It is an optional paid add-on, not an MT5 EA importer. Evaluations and initial funded accounts are simulated and plan rules still apply; we don’t claim the AI supplies a trading edge.
